meta.reportLabel: Wed - THE BOARD FLIPPED IN TWO PLACES OVERNIGHT. First, NEW ZEALAND BROKE: Q2 unemployment jumped to 5.6% against 5.4% expected, the highest since September 2015, underutilisation rose to 13.8% from 12.9% and the labour cost index slowed to 2.1% y/y. The September 2 hike is dead and the RBNZ cycle ended after one move - NZD collapses from +1 to -2 and AUD/NZD, NZD/CAD and NZD/CHF all REVERSE. Second, THE EURO GOT A REAL ENGINE: July flash HICP rose to 2.9% from 2.8% with core UP to 2.5%, services 3.3% and energy inflation 10%, while Q2 GDP printed +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y after a flat Q1, and the composite PMI hit 51.9 with services back at 51.6. The September 10 ECB hike no longer depends on oil - EUR goes to +2 and leads the board. Third, THE DOLLAR SOFTENED: JOLTS fell to 7.359m from 7.537m against 7.40m expected and DXY sits at 99.90, a seven-week low; USD drops to 0. WTI is down to $75.40 after a second heavy session, silver is testing $60.00 and the DAX made a record above 26,000. Cleanest trades: EUR/NZD LONG, GBP/NZD LONG, AUD/NZD LONG, EUR/CHF LONG. Next gate: US ADP 12:15Z and ISM services 14:00Z today, then July payrolls Friday.

meta.regime: Two legs of the board changed overnight and both changes are fundamental rather than positional. New Zealand printed a Q2 labour market report that ends its hiking cycle: unemployment climbed to 5.6% from 5.4% against a 5.4% consensus, the highest reading since September 2015, the underutilisation rate rose to 13.8% from 12.9%, and annual wage inflation on the labour cost index slowed to 2.1%. Employment did rise 0.5% q/q, but that came with participation jumping to 70.7% from 70.4%, which is what pushed the jobless rate up. The RBNZ hiked once on July 8 to 2.50% on a Q2 CPI of 4.1% that was 27.5% petrol - and crude has now fallen roughly 12% in two sessions, so the inflation impulse that justified that hike is being deleted at the same time the labour market cracks. NZD goes from +1 to -2 and every kiwi cross reverses. Against that, the euro acquired the one thing it was missing. July flash HICP came in at 2.9% from 2.8% with core UP to 2.5% from 2.4%, services inflation 3.3% and energy inflation at 10%; Q2 GDP grew 0.4% q/q and 1.0% y/y after a flat Q1; and the July composite PMI printed 51.9 with services back in expansion at 51.6 from 49.4. Until yesterday the roughly 70% pricing of a September 10 ECB hike rested entirely on the oil surge Lagarde had flagged, which made it hostage to Hormuz. It now rests on domestic prices and domestic growth, so cheaper crude no longer collapses it. EUR moves to +2 and leads the board. The dollar meanwhile lost the thread: JOLTS job openings fell to 7.359 million from 7.537 million against a 7.40 million forecast, yields retreated, and DXY sits near 99.90 at a seven-week low even after Monday's 55.6 ISM manufacturing print. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said underlying inflation remains too high and policy needs to stay mildly restrictive, adding that current settings likely already meet that description - hawkish in tone, but a hold in substance. USD falls to 0 into Friday's payrolls.
meta.nextBigEvent: US July employment report, Friday Aug 7 12:30Z (consensus +91k after +57k)

dailyRead: Trade the two reversals and leave the dollar alone until Friday. New Zealand is the big one: Q2 unemployment at 5.6% against 5.4% expected is the highest since September 2015, underutilisation widened to 13.8% from 12.9%, and the labour cost index slowed to 2.1% y/y - there is no wage-price pressure left to justify a follow-up hike on September 2, and the Q2 CPI of 4.1% that got the RBNZ moving in the first place was 27.5% petrol at a moment when WTI has just fallen roughly 12% in two sessions to $75.40. The kiwi drops from +1 to -2 and the crosses invert: AUD/NZD flips from SHORT to LONG, NZD/CAD and NZD/CHF flip from LONG to SHORT, and the cleanest expressions of the whole move are EUR/NZD LONG and GBP/NZD LONG where a hawkish central bank faces one that has just been stopped. The second change is the euro, and it is the more durable of the two. July flash HICP rose to 2.9% with core UP to 2.5%, services at 3.3% and energy inflation running at 10%, while Q2 GDP came in at 0.4% q/q and 1.0% y/y after a flat first quarter and the composite PMI reached 51.9 with services back in expansion at 51.6. The September 10 hike was previously an oil trade that a Hormuz deal would have destroyed; it is now a domestic inflation and domestic growth trade that survives cheaper crude. That is the non-obvious shift on the board and it makes EUR/CHF LONG, EUR/JPY LONG and EUR/CAD LONG better trades today than they were yesterday. The dollar is the leg to avoid: JOLTS missed at 7.359 million against 7.40 million, DXY is at a seven-week low near 99.90, and Paulson talked hawkish while describing current policy as already appropriate - so EUR/USD at 1.1530 and GBP/USD at 1.3450 are RANGE into ADP at 12:15Z, ISM services at 14:00Z and Friday's payrolls, which is the only print that settles the September FOMC. On the yen, the intervention trade is fading exactly as the wage miss implied: USD/JPY has drifted back to 157.80 from the 155.39 spike and the yen was the only major to lose ground yesterday, so JPY comes off to 0 and USD/JPY becomes RANGE rather than SHORT - respect the MoF ceiling nearer 160 but stop paying for a trend that is not there. Oil is the one place to stand down entirely: the structural short has delivered two sessions of -7.4% and -5.3%, but the curve is deeply backwardated, Cushing stocks are tight, speculative positioning is light and an announcement is reportedly hours away, so USOIL goes to RANGE - the trade is made, do not press it. Gold at $4,096 and silver at $59.98 both keep rising against the peace trade because falling real rates matter more to them than the war does, and silver has the extra industrial leg from record equity risk appetite with the DAX above 26,000.

today.headline: Q2 unemployment 5.6% vs 5.4% expected - highest since Sept 2015, underutilisation 13.8%, labour cost index down to 2.1% y/y.
today.read: The September 2 hike is off and the RBNZ cycle is over after a single move, so the carry premium that made the kiwi a G10 long has been withdrawn rather than merely reduced. Sell NZD against EUR and GBP where the rate paths now diverge outright, and treat the AUD/NZD, NZD/CAD and NZD/CHF reversals as regime changes rather than pullbacks.

today.headline: July flash HICP 2.9% with core UP to 2.5%; Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y; composite PMI 51.9 with services back at 51.6.
today.read: The September 10 hike has stopped being a bet on the oil price and become a bet on domestic prices, which is a far more durable footing and the single most important repricing on the board. Buy the euro against the franc, the kiwi and the loonie; leave EUR/USD as a range until payrolls clears.

today.headline: JOLTS job openings fell to 7.359m from 7.537m against 7.40m expected; DXY at 99.90, a seven-week low.
today.read: Monday's 55.6 ISM gave the September dissenters a data point and Tuesday's JOLTS took it back, leaving Friday's payrolls as the only print that resolves it. Do not express any view through the dollar leg this week - use the crosses instead, where the divergences are actually clean.

today.headline: USD/JPY back to 157.80 from the 155.39 intervention spike; the yen was the only major to lose ground on Tuesday.
today.read: Without the wage story the joint operation is a ceiling and nothing more, and the ceiling is being tested a little further out each session. Stop paying for yen strength - USD/JPY becomes a range between the intervention line near 160 and the 155 spike low, and the JPY-cross shorts come off.

today.headline: WTI down to $75.40 after a second heavy session, with an Al Arabiya report that a Hormuz announcement could come within hours.
today.read: The loonie has no rates leg with both core measures under target, so cheaper crude keeps it pinned and USD/CAD, EUR/CAD and GBP/CAD stay long. But the oil move is now mature, so this is a hold-not-add: a formal announcement is the sell-the-fact risk in both crude and CAD.

today.headline: Led the majors on Tuesday, +0.66% against the dollar to reclaim 0.7050, on the improved risk backdrop and cheaper regional energy costs.
today.read: The RBA on Aug 11 is a consensus hold but the Q2 weighted median at 3.7% and services at 4.0% keep a hawkish statement live, and the Aussie now has a better relative position against the kiwi than it has had all year. Express AUD strength through AUD/NZD rather than AUD/USD into Friday.

today.headline: No change - July CPI at 0.4% with core 0.3% keeps the franc pinned at zero to 2027, thesis holds.
today.read: The franc remains the cleanest funding leg on the board now that the euro has a hardening rate path against it, and the SNB has committed only to leaning against appreciation. Stay long EUR/CHF and GBP/CHF; the only thing that caps them is a genuine haven flare out of Hormuz.

today.headline: No change - cable at 1.3450 consolidating below the 1.3470 trendline, no domestic catalysts, thesis holds.
today.read: The hawkish 6-3 hold, 4.3% wage growth and a composite PMI at 52.1 mean the rates story is intact even though sterling has nothing to trade on this week. Buy it against the kiwi and the franc, not against the dollar or the euro.

USD.note: Held 3.50-3.75% on Jul 29 for a fifth straight meeting with THREE dissents FOR a hike, and Chair Warsh declined to give guidance or submit a dot. The hawkish case peaked with Monday's ISM manufacturing at 55.6 from 53.3 and has been leaking since: JOLTS job openings fell to 7.359m from 7.537m against 7.40m expected, with declines in healthcare, leisure, wholesale and business services. Philadelphia Fed President Paulson said underlying inflation is still too high and policy should stay mildly restrictive, but that current settings likely already qualify. June CPI 3.5%, core 2.6%, Q2 GDP 1.5%, payrolls +57k. July jobs on Aug 7 and July CPI on Aug 12 decide it.

EUR.note: Deposit facility 2.25% after the Jun 11 hike (refi 2.40%, MLF 2.65%), confirmed unchanged Jul 23. The case just hardened materially: July flash HICP 2.9% from 2.8%, core UP to 2.5% from 2.4%, services inflation 3.3% and energy inflation 10%. Growth turned as well - Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y after a flat Q1, with the July composite PMI at 51.9 and services back in expansion at 51.6 from 49.4. That removes the Hormuz dependency that made the September pricing fragile. Unemployment 6.3%, negotiated wages 2.46%.

GBP.note: Held 3.75% on Jul 30 but 6-3, a third member joining the dissent against a 7-2 consensus. June CPI 2.6%, core 2.6%, services 3.6%. The labour market is firmer than the pause implies - employment +148k in May, wages 4.3%, unemployment 4.9% - and July services PMI jumped to 51.8 from 48.8 with the composite at 52.1. Manufacturing was revised down to 51.9 from 52.5, which is the one soft spot. Cable at 1.3450 is capped by the downward-sloping trendline near 1.3470.

JPY.note: Held 1.00% on Jul 31 8-1, Takata dissenting for 1.25%. The wage leg has gone: June labour cash earnings rose just 2.5% y/y against 3.2% expected, after May slowed to 3.2% from 3.6%, and the July Outlook Report had already CUT FY2026 CPI to 2.5% from 2.8%. The one hawkish crumb is Tokyo July core CPI at 1.9% from 1.6% with ex-food-and-energy at 2.0%. The near-term yen driver remains fiscal, not monetary - the joint MoF and US Treasury operation and the pledge to repeat it - and that bid is visibly fading with USD/JPY back at 157.80.

AUD.note: Cash rate 4.35% after three hikes in 2026 (Feb, Mar, May) on the energy shock. Q2 trimmed mean 3.6% but the WEIGHTED MEDIAN ROSE to 3.7% from 3.5% and services inflation to 4.0% from 3.7%, which is not a pause profile. Against that, consumer inflation expectations dropped hard to 4.7% from 5.5% in July and cheaper crude will pull Q3 CPI down. Unemployment 4.4% with employment +76.3k in June, services PMI 53.0 and composite 52.6. TE's model still carries 4.60%; the market and all four majors expect no change.

NZD.note: OCR raised 25bp to 2.50% on Jul 8, the first hike in three years, with further increases described as possible. That is now finished. Q2 unemployment printed 5.6% against 5.4% expected, up from 5.4%, the highest since September 2015; underutilisation widened to 13.8% from 12.9%; and the labour cost index slowed to 2.1% y/y. Employment rose 0.5% q/q but only because participation climbed to 70.7% from 70.4%. The Q2 CPI of 4.1% that triggered July's move was 27.5% petrol, and crude is down roughly 12% in two sessions. Two-year inflation expectations 2.53%.

CAD.note: Held 2.25% on Jul 15 for a sixth straight meeting. June CPI cooled to 2.8% from 3.2% with CPI-trim 1.8% and CPI-median 1.9%, BOTH BELOW target, as gasoline decelerated from +33.2% y/y. Q1 GDP 0.0% q/q and -0.1% y/y, unemployment 6.6% after a +87.8k employment rebound. There is no rates leg at all, so the loonie is a pure terms-of-trade trade - and its terms of trade are being repriced in Muscat rather than Ottawa.

CHF.note: At ZERO since mid-2025, held Dec, Mar and Jun; panellists see no change until 2027. July CPI came in at 0.4% y/y against 0.5% expected, down from 0.5%, with core unchanged at 0.3% - under the SNB's own 0.7% Q3 conditional forecast. Producer and import prices are deflating at -2.1% y/y and unemployment is 2.9%. FX reserves rose to CHF 758.8bn in June from 710.9bn, a CHF 47.9bn build consistent with intervention. The June statement pledged to lean against rapid APPRECIATION only; the SNB is content to let the franc slide.

The next question for the RBNZ is how long it holds, not how far it goes. symbols.why: The widest gap on the board at four points. An ECB whose September hike just acquired a domestic inflation and growth case - July core HICP 2.5%, Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q - against an RBNZ whose cycle ended overnight with unemployment at a decade high of 5.6% and wage growth down to 2.1%.
symbols.risk: A hot US payroll on Friday lifts the dollar against both legs and can compress the cross; a partial retracement of the kiwi jobless rate as participation normalises is the domestic counter.

symbols.why: A BoE with three dissenters for a hike, 4.3% wage growth and services PMI back at 51.8 against a central bank that has just been stopped by a 5.6% unemployment print. Three-point score gap and the two rate paths now point in opposite directions.
symbols.risk: Sterling has no domestic catalyst this week and cable keeps rejecting 1.3470, so the pair depends entirely on the kiwi leg continuing to sell off.

symbols.why: The clean policy-gap trade, now with the gap widening in expectation as well as level: an ECB deposit rate at 2.25% with a September hike backed by core HICP accelerating to 2.5%, against an SNB at zero whose July CPI at 0.4% undershot its own 0.7% Q3 forecast with import prices deflating at -2.1%.
symbols.risk: A haven flare if the Hormuz announcement fails to arrive bids the franc regardless of the rate gap, and the SNB's appreciation-only pledge means it will not lean against a euro-driven fall in the cross.

symbols.why: REVERSED from SHORT. The entire basis of yesterday's short was an RBNZ that might hike again on Sept 2 against an RBA on hold - that basis is gone. Australia keeps the 185bp rate advantage plus a Q2 weighted median rising to 3.7%, while New Zealand posts its worst labour report in a decade.
symbols.risk: The RBA on Aug 11 is the immediate event and a dovish statement off the collapse in consumer inflation expectations to 4.7% from 5.5% would take the hawkish tail out of the Aussie leg.

symbols.why: Unemployment at 5.6% against 5.4% expected removes the only reason the kiwi was bid, and the pair had already stalled near 0.5871 ahead of the release. The carry story that supported it through July no longer exists.
symbols.risk: The dollar is the weak side of this pair too - DXY at a seven-week low after the JOLTS miss - so a soft ADP today or a soft payroll Friday cushions the kiwi even on bad domestic news.

symbols.why: Two-point gap. A kiwi that has lost its hiking cycle against a yen that still has an official bid and a stated pledge to repeat it, even if that bid is fading.
symbols.risk: The yen leg is the weaker half of the thesis - USD/JPY has already drifted back to 157.80 and JPY was the only major to lose ground on Tuesday, so this relies mostly on kiwi weakness.

symbols.why: 1.1530 after recovering Monday's loss on the JOLTS miss, holding comfortably above 1.1500. The euro leg improved materially on the HICP and GDP data but the dollar leg is a coin flip until Friday, so the two-point score gap is not tradeable yet.
symbols.risk: This is the pair that most deserves a directional long once payrolls clears - a miss below +91k likely breaks it higher, a beat sends it back to test 1.1500.

symbols.why: A euro with accelerating core inflation and a September hike case, against a yen whose only support is a fading level defence and whose wage data killed the BoJ leg. The rebound is stalling below the 200-day SMA, so entry matters.
symbols.risk: A second joint MoF and US Treasury operation would hit this hard and fast - the yen leg is administrative, which means it can move without warning.

symbols.why: Three-point gap. Both currencies were levered to oil but in opposite directions, and the euro just broke that link - its hike pricing now rests on domestic core inflation rather than the energy premium, while CAD has no rates leg at all with both core measures under target.
symbols.risk: The oil sell-off is mature at $75.40 with a backwardated curve and light positioning, so a crude snapback helps CAD immediately and the euro not at all.

symbols.why: WTI down from $84 to $75.40 in two sessions against a BoC on its sixth hold with CPI-trim at 1.8% and CPI-median at 1.9%. The loonie has no domestic support to offset a terms-of-trade hit of this size.
symbols.risk: The dollar leg is soft - DXY at a seven-week low after JOLTS - so this is a CAD-weakness trade rather than a USD-strength trade, and a formal Hormuz announcement is a sell-the-fact risk in crude.

symbols.why: The 6-3 hawkish hold, 4.3% wage growth and a composite PMI at 52.1 give sterling a live rates story against a franc pinned at zero until 2027 with July CPI undershooting its own central bank forecast at 0.4%.
symbols.risk: Sterling has no domestic catalyst this week, and a haven bid out of a failed Hormuz announcement lifts the franc leg regardless of the policy gap.

symbols.why: A 150bp policy gap still widening in direction - a BoE with three dissenters for a hike against a BoC with nothing to do and its only driver, crude, down 12% in two sessions.
symbols.risk: Both legs are quiet domestically, so this trades entirely off oil; a crude rebound reverses it faster than any UK data could support it.

symbols.why: A 435bp nominal carry, the widest in the G10, with the Aussie leading the majors on Tuesday and a Q2 weighted median that rose to 3.7%, against a franc at zero with core inflation stuck at 0.3%.
symbols.risk: A dovish RBA on Aug 11 off the drop in inflation expectations to 4.7% would undercut the carry story, and a haven flare hits high-beta-versus-franc trades hardest.

symbols.why: A 210bp rate gap with a live hawkish tail at the RBA against a BoC with core measures under target, and the crude collapse lands squarely on the CAD leg while Australia benefits from cheaper regional energy input costs.
symbols.risk: Both are commodity currencies exposed to the same global growth impulse, and an oil rebound helps CAD far more directly than the RBA could help AUD.

symbols.why: Silver at $59.98 testing $60.00 after surging 2.5% on Tuesday, the strongest momentum on the board. Falling real rates from the JOLTS miss plus an industrial demand leg powered by record equity risk appetite - the DAX above 26,000 and record US closes.
symbols.risk: The industrial leg cuts both ways: a strong payroll on Friday that re-arms the September hike lifts real rates and would decouple silver lower from gold rather than higher, and $60 is an obvious profit-taking level.

symbols.why: A record above 26,000 on Aug 4, up more than 1.5%, on the crude collapse, strong corporate earnings including Siemens Healthineers up over 6% on raised guidance, and the ongoing AI technology rebound.
symbols.risk: The euro-area data that made the DAX rally possible is the same data that hardens the ECB's September hike - a hawkish repricing plus an oil snapback is the double headwind, and the index is already at a record.

symbols.why: REVERSED from SHORT. The euro leg changed: July core HICP accelerating to 2.5% and Q2 GDP at +0.4% q/q give the ECB a case sterling's committee already had, and the ECB is the one with an actual hike priced for September.
symbols.risk: Only a one-point score gap, and the BoE's 6-3 vote with 4.3% wage growth means sterling's hawkish tail is real - this is the lowest-conviction of the euro longs.

symbols.why: 1.3450 consolidating below the downward-sloping trendline near 1.3470, with no domestic catalysts leaving price action dictated entirely by the dollar. Score gap is only one point.
symbols.risk: Payrolls resolves it - a miss takes cable through 1.3470 toward 1.3500, a beat sends it back to the July range low.

symbols.why: REVERSED from SHORT. Climbed 0.60% to 0.7050 to reclaim the figure, leading the majors on the improved risk backdrop and cheaper regional energy, while the dollar lost its footing on the JOLTS miss.
symbols.risk: Two binaries inside a week - the RBA on Aug 11 where all four majors expect a hold, and US payrolls on Friday. Size accordingly and prefer AUD/NZD for the same view.

symbols.why: Downgraded from MEDIUM. The franc leg is unchanged and weak - zero until 2027, July CPI 0.4%, core 0.3% - but the dollar leg deteriorated with JOLTS and DXY at a seven-week low. The trendline break puts the 50-day SMA in focus.
symbols.risk: A soft ADP today or a soft payroll Friday hits the dollar leg while a haven bid lifts the franc leg - the two-sided invalidation, and the reason this is no longer a medium-conviction long.

symbols.why: Downgraded from SHORT. Back at 157.80 from the 155.39 spike, with the yen the only major to weaken on Tuesday and no BoJ engine after June wages missed at 2.5% against 3.2%. Both legs now score zero. Trade the band between the intervention line near 160 and the 155 spike low.
symbols.risk: A second joint operation caps it violently from above; a payroll beat on Friday pushes it into the MoF zone from below. Levels, not direction.

symbols.why: REVERSED from SHORT. Sterling's hawkish 6-3 hold and 4.3% wage growth against a yen whose intervention bid is fading and whose wage-price cycle just missed. One-point gap, so size small.
symbols.risk: This is the JPY cross most exposed to a second intervention because it is the highest-beta of the majors against the yen - the reversal is thesis-driven, not momentum-driven.

symbols.why: REVERSED from SHORT. The Aussie led the majors on Tuesday and gained 1.02% against the yen specifically, the largest single move in the majors grid, as the intervention premium bled out.
symbols.risk: A one-point score gap between two currencies with events inside a week - RBA Aug 11 on one side, a possible second MoF operation on the other.

symbols.why: One-point gap. The euro has the harder catalyst - a September hike now backed by core inflation at 2.5% - while the RBA is a consensus hold with an argument rather than a decision behind it.
symbols.risk: The Aussie was the strongest major on Tuesday and has its own hawkish tail in the Q2 weighted median at 3.7%, so this is a slow grind rather than a momentum trade.

symbols.why: Downgraded hard from HIGH. CAD at -1 with crude at $75.40 and no rates leg still argues for the short, but the yen leg has collapsed as a thesis - JPY is now 0, not +2, and the one-point gap does not support the size a two-day-old HIGH implied.
symbols.risk: Both legs can rally together: an oil snapback rebuilds CAD at the same moment a quiet MoF lets the yen slide. Take profit rather than hold for extension.

symbols.why: Downgraded from HIGH. Swiss July CPI at 0.4% under the SNB's own 0.7% forecast with the rate at zero is still the better fundamental short, but with JPY at 0 the gap is one point rather than three.
symbols.risk: Both are haven currencies, so a failed Hormuz announcement bids them together and the cross goes nowhere - and the franc would likely move first, since its bid is organic rather than administrative.

symbols.why: REVERSED from LONG. The rates-plus-terms-of-trade divergence that made this a long has inverted on one side - the RBNZ is finished hiking after a 5.6% unemployment print, while the BoC was already on hold.
symbols.risk: One-point gap between two weak currencies, and the CAD leg is hostage to a crude market where the sell-off looks mature - a bounce in oil is the fastest way to lose this.

symbols.why: REVERSED from LONG. Yesterday this was the cleanest carry pair on the board on an RBNZ that might reach 2.75%; the Q2 labour report removed that outright, leaving a one-point gap between two weakening currencies.
symbols.risk: The franc is only 250bp cheaper in carry terms and the SNB wants it weaker, so this pair pays nothing to hold - it is a thesis trade with negative carry, which caps how long to run it.

symbols.why: 99.90 at a seven-week low after the JOLTS miss, and the index's largest weight by far - EUR at 57.6% - is the strongest currency on the board following the HICP and GDP upgrades. JPY at 13.6% is neutral rather than supportive.
symbols.risk: Friday's payrolls is a genuine two-way binary on this index specifically; a beat above +91k re-arms the September hike and clears 100 decisively.

symbols.why: STOOD DOWN from SHORT. The structural short has paid twice over - $84 to $75.40 across two sessions of -7.4% and -5.3% - and Al Arabiya reports a Hormuz announcement could come within hours. But the curve is deeply backwardated, Cushing stocks are tight and speculative positioning is light, all of which warn the sell-off has run ahead of the physical market. The trade is made; do not press it.
symbols.risk: Two-way from here. Below $70 if the strait genuinely reopens and traffic flows as it briefly did in early July; a violent squeeze above $84 if the announcement slips again, which it has done repeatedly since Feb 28.

symbols.why: Upgraded from RANGE. Gold at $4,096, up again after +0.6% on Tuesday to $4,080, rising through a de-escalation tape because falling real rates matter more to it than the war does - the JOLTS miss pulled yields down and the dollar to a seven-week low.
symbols.risk: $4,100 has capped it twice this week, and a payroll beat that revives the September hike would lift real rates and hit the haven leg simultaneously.

symbols.why: JPY classified MIXED at 0, so the basket is a range rather than a directional ticket - the opposite side of the USD/JPY range call. Downgraded from LONG on the wage miss and the fade back to 157.80.
symbols.risk: Binary in both directions: a second joint operation sends it sharply higher, continued silence lets it bleed back toward the pre-intervention lows.

symbols.why: Both score +1. A BoE drifting hawkish with three dissenters against an RBA with a rising weighted median but a consensus hold - two similar stories with no score gap to trade.
symbols.risk: The RBA on Aug 11 is the only thing that separates them this week, and it cuts either way.

symbols.why: Both currencies score -1 and both are weakening for unrelated reasons - CAD on the crude collapse, CHF on an inflation undershoot and a central bank that wants it lower. No edge either way.
symbols.risk: The two legs respond to opposite Hormuz outcomes: a real reopening lifts the franc relatively, a failed announcement lifts CAD via oil - and both could happen inside a week.

catalysts.event: Hormuz announcement reportedly imminent — Iran still denies talking to Washington
catalysts.note: Al Arabiya and Al Hadath, citing high-level sources, reported that an announcement on the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz could come within hours, with communications underway at full tilt. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there has been progress but not finality and that he hopes an agreement will happen very shortly. Iran continues to insist it is not negotiating with the United States at all - foreign ministry spokesman Baghaei says the talks are with Oman, over a NEW maritime route separate from existing corridors, and Foreign Minister Araghchi has stated that such an agreement does not mean the reopening of the strait. Trump called Iran's leadership unbelievably duplicitous after that denial. The strait has been effectively closed since the war began Feb 28; WTI traded below $70 when traffic briefly flowed in early July. This is the swing factor over USOIL, XAU, CAD, GER40 and the whole CHF block, and it is now a sell-the-fact risk in crude rather than a further-downside catalyst.

catalysts.event: Joint US-Japan FX intervention — the bid is fading
catalysts.note: Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama confirmed the MoF purchased yen in coordination with the US Treasury, the first joint operation since 2011, executed under the September 2025 Joint Statement of the Japanese and US Finance Ministers and aimed at excessive volatility and disorderly movements. Both sides pledged not to hesitate to conduct further coordinated interventions. USD/JPY spiked to 155.39 from above 163 - and has since drifted back to 157.80, with the yen the only major to lose ground on Tuesday. June labour cash earnings at +2.5% y/y against +3.2% expected removed the monetary leg. Size yen shorts for the possibility of a second operation; do not size yen longs as though a trend exists.

catalysts.event: Euro area final services and composite PMIs
catalysts.note: Germany's services reading is expected to be confirmed at 49.6, still in contraction, with the German composite at 51.2 and the euro area composite unchanged at 51.9. Spain's services index is forecast at 55.3 from 54.2. After the Q2 GDP upgrade to +0.4% q/q these are confirmations rather than surprises, but a downward revision to the euro area composite would take some of the shine off the new ECB hike case.

Annual factory-gate inflation is forecast to slow sharply to 4.6% from 5.9%. This is the first place the crude collapse shows up in euro area data, and it is the counterargument to yesterday's hawkish HICP - if pipeline pressure is deflating this fast, the 10% energy-inflation print in the July flash is a base effect that unwinds into the autumn.

Private hiring is expected to slow to 70k in July from 98k in June. It matters more than usual after the JOLTS miss took openings down to 7.359m - two consecutive soft labour reads would effectively pre-empt Friday and kill the September hike the three July dissenters want. A beat is the dollar's only route back above DXY 100 before payrolls.

Forecast to edge up to 54.5 from 54.0, with prices paid last at 67.7 and the employment index at 51.2. The employment sub-index is the number to watch given JOLTS: services is where the openings declines were concentrated, in healthcare, leisure and hospitality and business services. Fed Governor Cook also speaks today.

The deficit is expected to narrow to AUD 1,100 million from 3,018 million. Relevant to the AUD/NZD long that is now the cleanest antipodean expression - Australia's terms of trade are the offset to a softer commodity complex, and a wider deficit would undercut the Aussie leg ahead of the RBA on Aug 11.

The biggest scheduled gate on the board and the only print that settles the dollar's direction. Consensus +91k after June's +57k, unemployment expected 4.3% from 4.2%, with April and May already revised down 74k combined. A second sub-100k print kills the September hike outright and breaks the dollar despite Monday's 55.6 ISM; a clean beat re-arms it and turns every RANGE call on the dollar legs into a directional short of EUR/USD and GBP/USD.

All four major Australian banks expect a hold at 4.35%, but the internals argue otherwise: the Q2 weighted median ROSE to 3.7% from 3.5%, services inflation to 4.0% from 3.7%, and July PMIs printed services 53.0 and composite 52.6. Against that, consumer inflation expectations collapsed to 4.7% from 5.5% in July and cheaper crude will pull Q3 CPI lower. This is now the key event for AUD/NZD, which reversed to LONG today.

TE forecasts 3.4% headline after June's 3.5%, with core last at 2.6%. Energy drove over 60% of a recent monthly gain, so whether the Hormuz premium actually comes out of crude feeds straight into this print and into the September FOMC decision. ISM prices paid at 71.1 says cost pressure is still in the pipeline.
Warsh's first Jackson Hole as Chair, and the venue where he would have to justify a September move after refusing to give guidance or submit a dot at the July press conference. Runs Aug 27-28.

The hike is off. After Q2 unemployment printed 5.6% against 5.4% expected - the highest since September 2015 - with underutilisation at 13.8% and the labour cost index at 2.1%, the OCR stays at 2.50%. The interest is entirely in the language: whether the Bank retains any tightening bias, or acknowledges that the petrol-driven 4.1% Q2 CPI is unwinding with crude at $75.

A seventh consecutive hold at 2.25% is the base case with CPI-trim 1.8% and CPI-median 1.9%, both under target. The interest is whether the Bank acknowledges that cheaper crude removes the energy contribution that has been holding headline CPI up at 2.8%, which would open the door to a cut and take CAD lower still.

Roughly 70% of a hike is priced and, after July's flash HICP at 2.9% with core UP to 2.5% and Q2 GDP at +0.4% q/q, that pricing finally has a domestic foundation rather than depending on the oil premium Lagarde flagged. Services inflation 3.3%, energy inflation 10%, composite PMI 51.9. The counterargument is producer prices, forecast to decelerate to 4.6% from 5.9% today.

Held 3.50-3.75% on Jul 29 with three dissents FOR a hike and no guidance or dot from Warsh. The hawkish case rests on ISM manufacturing at 55.6 and is being undermined by the labour data - JOLTS at 7.359m and payrolls at +57k. July jobs and July CPI both land first and will decide it.

TE forecasts a hold at 3.75%, but the Jul 30 vote was 6-3 against a 7-2 consensus and July services PMI swung back into expansion at 51.8 with the composite at 52.1. A fourth dissenter would confirm sterling's hawkish tail; the downwardly revised manufacturing PMI at 51.9 is the counterargument.

A hold at 1.00% is the firm base case - the July Outlook Report cut FY2026 CPI to 2.5% from 2.8% and June wages missed at 2.5% against 3.2% expected - with Oct or Dec the live window. Takata is already dissenting for 1.25% and Tamura wants a neutral rate near 2%. Tokyo July core CPI at 1.9% from 1.6% is the one datapoint arguing the other way.

A hold at 0% is universally expected, with panellists seeing no change until 2027 and July CPI at 0.4% undershooting the Bank's own 0.7% Q3 conditional forecast. The relevance is language: the June statement pledged to lean against rapid franc APPRECIATION only, and any hardening of that is the main cap on EUR/CHF and GBP/CHF.

geopolitics: The Hormuz standoff has reached the point where the announcement itself is the risk rather than the delay. Al Arabiya and Al Hadath, citing high-level sources, reported on Tuesday that a statement on reopening the strait could come within hours, with communications underway at full tilt - and WTI fell another 5.3% on that report alone, to $75.80 on Tuesday and $75.40 on Wednesday, after Monday's 7.4% collapse. Brent is back under $80. But the two sides are still describing different negotiations. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there has been progress made but not finality on an agreement for free transit, and that he hopes it will happen very shortly. Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei says Tehran is not negotiating with the United States at all: its talks are with Oman, assessed positively at both technical and political levels, and focused on establishing a NEW maritime route separate from existing corridors that protects both countries' sovereign rights. Foreign Minister Araghchi has said those negotiations are in their final stages while stating explicitly that an agreement does not mean the reopening of the strait. Trump responded to the denial by calling Iran's leadership unbelievably duplicitous, having previously described the talks as Tehran's last chance. The strait has been effectively closed since the war began on Feb 28, and when traffic briefly flowed in early July WTI traded below $70. So the direction of travel is de-escalation and the market has now priced roughly 12% of it in two sessions. The transmission into FX has changed shape today in one important respect: the euro used to be the main casualty of a reopening, because the ECB's September hike pricing was built on the oil surge Lagarde named as an upside inflation risk. July's flash HICP at 2.9% with core UP to 2.5%, and Q2 GDP at +0.4% q/q, have given that hike a domestic case instead - which means the euro is no longer a levered short on peace. What remains directly exposed is CAD, which has no rates leg at all with both BoC core measures under target, and NZD, whose Q2 CPI of 4.1% was 27.5% petrol and whose central bank has just been stopped by a 5.6% unemployment print. On crude itself the risk has become two-sided: a deeply backwardated curve, tight Cushing stocks and light speculative positioning all warn the sell-off has run ahead of the physical market, which is why USOIL comes off SHORT to RANGE. Gold at $4,096 and silver at $59.98 both continue to rise against the peace tape, which says the metals are trading US real rates rather than the war - and that is the more reliable signal into Friday's payrolls.
